newsitem.title: USA: Magellan cut bond holdings but only moderately.
newsitem.headline: Magellan cut bond holdings but only moderately.

text.p: In his first two months at the helm of Fidelity Investments Magellan Fund, Bob Stansky has shed the fund's massive stake in bonds at a slower rate than many fund-watchers expected.

Fidelity said Thursday that Magellan, the nation's largest mutual fund, cut its stake in bonds to 15.6 percent of assets at the end of July, down from 18.1 percent at the end of June and 19.3 percent at the end of May when Stansky took over.
"He's going a lot slower than I expected him to," said David O'Leary, president of Alpha Equity Research of Portsmouth, N.H.

Stansky boosted the fund's stock holdings to 82.8 percent of the portfolio at the end of July from 79.0 percent at the same time in June, according to Fidelity's Internet site (http://www.fid-inv.com).
He cut cash and other investments to just 1.5 percent of assets at the end of July, the most recent month figures are available, from 2.8 percent at the end of June.

Many analysts said in May that Stansky would quickly slash Magellan's massive holdings in bonds when took the helm in June from former manager Jeffrey Vinik, who was widely criticised for his move into bonds and the fund's recent poor performance.
However, U.S. bonds and notes remained in the top three positions of Magellan's top 10 largest holdings at the end of July and the fund still had more than $8 billion invested in U.S. Treasuries.

At the beginning of August, Fidelity said on its Internet site that Stansky was "proceeding deliberately" in reviewing the fund and the second quarter earnings season would be important for determing Magellan's direction.
Stansky was not available to comment on Thursday.
O'Leary said Stansky may be averaging out of bonds by selling $50 million to $100 million or so a day of the more than $8 billion invested in U.S. treasuries.
"Vinik got it wrong by buying them, and if (Stansky) blew them out all at once, and rates topped and started to decline, Magellan shareholders would lose twice," he said.
The company also said the assets of the Magellan Fund rose to $51.683 billion at the end of August and to $51.913 billion on Sept. 4 from $50.972 billion at the end of July.
Analysts said investors continued to redeem shares in the massive mutual fund, though at a slower pace than in recent months.
Eric Kobren, publisher of Fidelity Insight, said he estimated that investors redeemed $580 million to $600 million in August, "which was less than what we saw in May, June or July."
"I think we're pretty safe that assets will stabilise here," Kobren said. "Investors should sort of sit tight and not pay as much attention to it as the media does."

Kobren estimated that investors have redeemed $3.9 billion from Magellan since April and a total of $2.4 billion year-to-date as news of the fund's recent poor performance and change in fund managers became widely reported.
The closely-watched mutual fund raised its holdings in energy stocks, its largest sector holding, to 13.8 percent of assets at the end of July from 13.5 percent at the end of June.
Stocks in durables rose to 10.8 percent from 10.4 percent, industrial machinery and equipment remained unchanged at 9.2 percent and finance rose to 7.0 percent from 6.6 percent.
Magellan dropped AT&T Corp. and a 30-year bond paying 7.625 percent from its top 10 holdings and added Royal Dutch Petroleum Co. and Exxon Corp.
